newsitem.title: DOMINICAN REPUBLIC: Peru, Dominican Republic discuss rebel asylum.
newsitem.headline: Peru, Dominican Republic discuss rebel asylum.

text.p: Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori discussed the possibility of asylum in the Dominican Republic for Marxist rebels in a meeting with President Leonel Fernandez on Sunday, a government source said.

Fujimori flew in to Santo Domingo on Sunday afternoon for a lightning trip to talk about the crisis in Lima where 20-odd Marxist guerrillas have been holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's residence for 75 days.

Asked whether Fujimori and Fernandez spoke of a possible Dominican asylum for the rebels in a 3 1/2 hour meeting, a source close to Fernandez said, "We are discussing that possibility but there is nothing concrete yet."
But, in a brief joint communique, Fernandez's office said only that the presidents had touched on the hostage crisis.

"President Fujimori gave a brief explanation of the current situation of the talks between the Peruvian government negotiator and the representatives of the MRTA (Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement) guerrillas," the statement read.
It added that Fernandez told Fujimori of the Dominican experience in similar cases.
Dominican Interior Minister Norge Botello said before Fujimori arrived that the Dominican Republic would be prepared to offer the guerrillas asylum if Peru requested it.
But Fujimori said in an interview broadcast on Peruvian television that the Dominican Republic would not be a likely destination for the rebels.
"I don't think the Dominican Republic will be acceptable to them (rebels) as a destination," Fujimori said.
"It's possible that in a third country at some moment it may be necessary and so we're talking about that in an informal way," he added.

News reports have suggested Cuba, Nicaragua or Eastern Europe as possible refuges in a deal to end Latin America's longest hostage siege. Fujimori said he has not spoken to Cuba's President Fidel Castro about asylum for the guerrillas.
It was his second visit to the Dominican Republic in less than a month. He met Fernandez during a surprise four-hour stopover at Santo Domingo airport on Feb. 5 on his way back from a trip to Canada.

The heavily-armed squad of Cuban-inspired guerrillas stormed a cocktail party at the Japanese ambassador's residence on Dec. 17. They swiftly freed hundreds of hostages but still hold two of Fujimori's relatives, the envoys of Japan and Bolivia, and two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats.
